### 1. Audit Shows Questionable Payments at Health and Human Services
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/audit-shows-questionable-payments-at-health-and-human-services-2026
- original_report_source_url: https://www.nd.gov/auditor/news/audit-shows-questionable-payments-health-and-human-services

- publisher_name: North Dakota Office of the State Auditor
- audit_organization: North Dakota Office of the State Auditor
- source_jurisdiction: North Dakota
- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: North Dakota
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 10
- publication_day: 29

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit examined DHHS's controls over program integrity and payment integrity for the 2023-2025 biennium, identifying weaknesses in provider engagement, EVV usage, background checks, and program eligibility; future audits should prioritize strengthening verification mechanisms, standardizing processes across divisions, and increasing data-driven monitoring to prevent similar improper payments.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
The audit identified several weaknesses in DHHS controls leading to seven areas of concern with millions of dollars in questionable payments, and highlighted gaps in provider engagement, verification, and data utilization. Strengthened governance, standardized processes, and data-driven monitoring are needed to prevent future improper payments.

#### llm_insight
The ND Office of the State Auditor's audit of DHHS identifies multiple control gaps that allowed substantial improper payments, particularly around program engagement, EVV verification, background checks, and eligibility, underscoring the need for stronger procedures and data-driven monitoring.

### 3. State High-Risk Program Assessment of Department of Health Care Services Oversight of Medi-Cal Provider Payments
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/state-high-risk-program-assessment-of-department-of-health-care-services-oversight-of-medi-cal-provider-payments-2026
- original_report_source_url: https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/2025-605
- publisher_key: california-state-auditor
- publisher_name: California State Auditor
- audit_organization: California State Auditor
- source_jurisdiction: California
- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: California
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 10
- publication_day: 15

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This assessment advances the objective of evaluating Health Care Services’ oversight of Medi-Cal provider payments by outlining significant weaknesses in follow-up on high-risk providers, ineligible-provider sanctions, and ground transportation fraud, while recognizing DHCS’s data-driven program integrity approach. It sets the stage for future in-depth audits that will test the effectiveness of analytics-driven triage, cross-agency data sharing, and corrective actions to reduce the risk of improper Medi-Cal payments.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
The California State Auditor concludes that Health Care Services’ oversight of Medi-Cal provider payments is at substantial risk of fraud, waste, or abuse due to inadequate follow-up on high-risk providers, ongoing participation of ineligible providers, and significant ground-transportation related overpayments; the assessment justifies updating Health Care Services’ inclusion on the state high-risk list and informs future targeted audits, but it is not the result of a state high-risk audit and does not include formal recommendations.

#### llm_insight
An evidence-based, multi-tool analytics approach is being used to flag potential issues, but the report emphasizes that risk indicators are signals needing corroboration through further research; the DOI demonstrates substantial program integrity investments and cross-agency collaboration, suggesting future audits should prioritize validating signals and streamlining data-sharing to maximize recovery.

### 5. South Carolina Did Not Report Approximately $108.6 Million of the Federal Share of Medicaid and CHIP Collections Subject to the Increased COVID-19 Federal Medical Assistance Percentage
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/south-carolina-did-not-report-approximately-108-6-million-of-the-federal-share-of-medicaid-and-chip-collections-0347b78c
- original_report_source_url: https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2026/south-carolina-did-not-report-approximately-1086-million-of-the-federal-share-of-medicaid-and-chip-collections-subject-to-the-increased-covid-19-federal-medical-assistance-percentage
- publisher_key: hhs-oig
- publisher_name: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General
- audit_organization: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General
- source_jurisdiction: Federal
- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: South Carolina
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 10
- publication_day: 2

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit evaluated whether South Carolina accurately calculated and reported the Federal share of Medicaid and CHIP collections subject to the increased COVID-19 FMAP during the audit period. It found underreporting of about $108.6 million and issued four recommendations to adjust CMS reports, refund amounts, and strengthen reporting policies for future FMAP changes.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
South Carolina did not accurately calculate and report the Federal share of Medicaid and CHIP collections subject to the increased COVID-19 FMAP during the audit period, resulting in underreporting of approximately $108.6 million; four recommendations were issued to CMS and the State to correct and prevent future misstatements.

#### llm_insight
The audit highlights the risk of misapplying COVID-19-related FMAP increases to Medicaid and CHIP collections and underscores the need for stronger internal controls, explicit policies, and clear CMS reporting procedures to ensure accurate Federal shares.

- subject_jurisdictions: none
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
CMS did not provide adequate oversight of States’ use of contract surveyors to conduct nursing home surveys, increasing the risk that contract surveyors do not meet Federal requirements; CMS concurred with the recommendations.

### 7. Oregon Health Authority: Medicaid Duplicate IDs Put Federal Funding at Risk
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/oregon-health-authority-medicaid-duplicate-ids-put-federal-funding-at-risk-2026
- original_report_source_url: https://sos.oregon.gov/audits/Pages/audit-2026-26-OHA.aspx
- publisher_key: oregon-audits-division
- publisher_name: Oregon Secretary of State, Audits Division
- audit_organization: Oregon Secretary of State Audits Division
- source_jurisdiction: Oregon
- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: Oregon
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit evaluated whether the Oregon Health Authority paid duplicate Medicaid capitation payments to the same recipient concurrently from 2020 to 2024, identified 645 potential duplicates with $230,252 in overpayments and projected total duplicate payments ranging from $232,000 to $4.1 million across the program, and concluded that corrective actions and strengthened data controls are needed to protect federal funding; the Oregon Secretary of State’s Audits Division issued rec­ommendations that OHA agreed to.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
OHA agreed with all recommendations.

#### llm_insight
The audit identifies duplicate Medicaid capitation payments to the same recipient during 2020–2024, highlighting risks to federal funding and underscoring the need for data governance, staff training, and system improvements to prevent and detect duplicates and to ensure proper reconciliation with federal requirements.

### 8. Alabama Medicaid Fraud Control Unit: 2025 Inspection
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/alabama-medicaid-fraud-control-unit-2025-inspection-2026
- original_report_source_url: Manual Upload: OEI-04-25-00400.pdf
- publisher_key: hhs-oig
- publisher_name: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General
- audit_organization: Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
- source_jurisdiction: Federal
- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: Alabama
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit evaluated whether the Alabama Medicaid Fraud Control Unit complied with grant requirements and performance standards during FYs 2023–2025, with attention to staffing adequacy, policy governance, referral flows from the PIU, case management, and cooperation with federal authorities. While the Unit demonstrated strengths in continuous case progression and collaboration with many Federal partners, it exhibited deficits in staffing levels, referral volumes, supervisory review documentation, and information management, leading to nine recommendations. OIG recertified the Unit in 2026 and noted concerns about staffing and referrals, indicating opportunities to strengthen operations for future audits.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
Overall, the Alabama MFCU generally performed in line with many standards and produced substantial case outcomes, but the inspection identified deficiencies in staffing, referral generation, case information management, and coordination with Federal partners. OIG recertified the Alabama MFCU on April 24, 2026, but noted two concerns that may limit effectiveness: staffing levels and adequacy of referrals.

#### llm_insight
The Alabama MFCU shows strengths in maintaining ongoing case progression and cooperative relationships with most Federal partners, but faces sustainability risks due to understaffing, inconsistent documentation of supervisory reviews, and limited referral flow from the PIU. Implementing a modern case management system, formalizing policy coordination with Federal partners, and expanding staff should improve timeliness and workload capacity, potentially increasing referrals and outcomes.

### 9. New York Medicaid Managed Care Capitation Payments for Incarcerated Enrollees
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/new-york-medicaid-managed-care-capitation-payments-for-incarcerated-enrollees-2026
- original_report_source_url: Manual Upload: OAS-25-02-074.pdf
- publisher_key: hhs-oig
- publisher_name: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General
- audit_organization: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General, Office of Audit Services
- source_jurisdiction: Federal
- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: New York
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit examined whether New York's Department of Health made unallowable capitation payments to Medicaid managed care organizations for incarcerated enrollees during 2021–2024, identified the total unallowable amounts not recovered, and concluded with recommendations to refund the federal share and strengthen disenrollment and data-matching controls to inform future audits of incarcerated populations in Medicaid.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
New York made unallowable managed care capitation payments totaling $7,551,670 ($6,164,734 Federal share) on behalf of 1,375 incarcerated Medicaid enrollees and did not consistently disenroll incarcerated enrollees; recommendations include refunding the Federal share and strengthening enrollment matching controls.

#### llm_insight
The report highlights risks from prolonged continuous enrollment during the PHE and data-matching gaps between prison incarceration data and Medicaid enrollment data, suggesting automated disenrollment triggers and enhanced, tolerance-based matching to prevent future unallowable capitation payments.

- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: Georgia
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit evaluated the Georgia MFCU’s performance over FYs 2021–2023, focusing on staffing, policies and procedures, referral management, case flow, information management, federal cooperation, and fiscal controls, to determine compliance with MFCU performance standards and identify improvement opportunities for future audits.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
The Georgia MFCU demonstrated active case progression and collaboration with federal partners, but faced persistent governance and control gaps, including staffing shortages, incomplete supervisory documentation, lack of formal equipment inventory policies, and delays in reporting convictions and adverse actions to OIG and NPDB. #### llm_insight

While case flow and interagency collaboration are strengths, sustained staffing and robust asset management practices are essential to improve compliance and program integrity.

### 11. South Carolina Did Not Report Approximately $108.6 Million of the Federal Share of Medicaid and CHIP Collections Subject to the Increased COVID-19 Federal Medical Assistance Percentage
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/south-carolina-did-not-report-approximately-108-6-million-of-the-federal-share-of-medicaid-and-chip-collections-03396cb0
- original_report_source_url: null
- publisher_key: hhs-oig
- publisher_name: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General
- audit_organization: Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General, Office of Audit Services
- source_jurisdiction: Federal
- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: South Carolina
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit evaluated whether South Carolina accurately calculated and reported the Federal share of Medicaid and CHIP collections subject to the increased COVID‑19 FMAP, for the period January 1, 2020, through March 31, 2025, and found underreporting linked to missing written policies and procedures; four recommendations were issued to align CMS reporting with accounting records and to establish controls for periods of unexpected or retroactive FMAP changes.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
The OIG determined that South Carolina did not accurately calculate and report the Federal share of Medicaid and CHIP collections subject to the increased COVID-19 FMAP during the audit period, resulting in underreporting of the Federal share (approximately $99.98 million, plus $8.59 million for the first quarter) and an overall overpayment of about $108.6 million to the State agency; lack of written policies and procedures contributed to reporting errors, prompting four recommendations to strengthen controls and FMAP-change handling.

#### llm_insight
The report highlights how retroactive FMAP changes and missing formal reporting procedures can lead to multi-million-dollar misstatements; implementing formal policies, reconciliations, and training is essential to reduce inaccuracies in CMS reporting.

- subject_jurisdictions: Tennessee
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
null

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
The OIG concluded that Tennessee claimed Federal Medicaid reimbursement for a subset of TCM services during FYs 2021–2023 that did not comply with Federal and State requirements, due to failure to verify eligibility for the designated target group and to assess TEIS cases properly. The estimated Federal overpayment totaled at least $59.3 million, and the report recommends refunds and procedural revisions. Tennessee did not concur with the recommendations.

#### llm_insight

### 13. Medicaid Managed Care: CMS’s Accuracy Check Process For State-Submitted MLR Data Has Limitations
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/medicaid-managed-care-cmss-accuracy-check-process-for-state-submitted-mlr-data-has-limitations-2026
- original_report_source_url: Manual Upload: OEI-03-23-00040.pdf
- publisher_key: cms
- publisher_name: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
- audit_organization: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
- source_jurisdiction: Federal
- jurisdiction_scope: national
- subject_jurisdictions: none
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit assesses CMS’s oversight activities to verify the accuracy of State-submitted Medicaid MLR data, focusing on the 2019 MLR reporting year and CMS’s five accuracy checks; it concludes that CMS conducted limited accuracy checks, did not follow up on identified potential inaccuracies, and did not share findings across relevant CMS staff, informing future audits to emphasize cross-team data sharing, internal procedures for material differences, and automated front-end checks to improve MLR data quality for capitation rate development.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
CMS’s oversight of State-submitted Medicaid MLR data has limitations due to reliance on optional data elements and lack of internal communication; while CMS has taken steps such as releasing an MLR Toolkit, implementing a web-based submission portal, and making MLR data public, the 2019 testing identified potential inaccuracies and missed follow-ups, indicating a need for enhanced procedures and internal sharing to improve data accuracy for capitation rate development.

#### llm_insight
The report highlights a data quality oversight gap: accuracy checks are incomplete because optional data elements are not consistently submitted, and findings are not shared across CMS teams, reducing their utility for rate setting. There are clear opportunities to introduce front-end automated checks and strengthened internal communication to improve Medicaid MLR data quality.

### 14. Wisconsin May Have Improperly Claimed $455 Million in Medicaid Reimbursement for Its School-Based Program
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/wisconsin-may-have-improperly-claimed-455-million-in-medicaid-reimbursement-for-its-school-based-program-2026-51793b93
- original_report_source_url: null
- publisher_key: hhs-oig
- publisher_name: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General
- audit_organization: Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General Office of Audit Services
- source_jurisdiction: Federal
- jurisdiction_scope: single_jurisdiction
- subject_jurisdictions: Wisconsin
- publication_year: 2026
- publication_month: 9
- publication_day: null

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit evaluated Wisconsin DHS's School-Based Services and Medicaid Administrative Claiming costs claimed for Federal Medicaid reimbursement for school years 2019–2022, focusing on RMTS coding accuracy, licensure verification, and IEP ratio-based cost allocation, and concluded that unallowable reimbursements may have been claimed totaling hundreds of millions of dollars, prompting six recommendations and plans to revise methodologies and sampling to ensure compliance in future audits.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
The State agency may have improperly claimed an estimated $454.9 million in Federal reimbursement through its Medicaid school-based program.

#### llm_insight
This audit highlights vulnerabilities in RMTS-based cost allocation, including missing student-identifying information, incomplete licensure verification, and privacy constraints around IEP data. The findings underscore the need for verifiable documentation and CMS-approved methodological improvements (SPA, RMTS implementation) to ensure future claims are eligible for Federal reimbursement and auditable.

#### llm_insight
This evaluation of the Georgia Medicaid Fraud Control Unit’s 2024 onsite inspection identified six open, unimplemented recommendations aimed at strengthening personnel practices, fraud referrals, supervisory documentation, reporting of convictions/adverse actions to federal partners, and equipment inventory controls.

### 19. Medicaid Managed Care: CMS’s Accuracy Check Process For State-Submitted Medical Loss Ratio Data Has Limitations
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/reports/medicaid-managed-care-cmss-accuracy-check-process-for-state-submitted-medical-loss-ratio-data-has-limitations-2026

#### objective (potential_objective_summary)
This audit evaluated CMS's verification of State-submitted Medicaid Medical Loss Ratio data, identified limitations in accuracy checks and follow-up, and recommended improvements to data sharing across CMS, to support more reliable capitation-rate decisions in future audits.

#### executive_summary (overall_conclusion)
The OIG identified limitations in CMS's process to verify State-submitted Medicaid MLR data and recommended procedures to address inaccuracies, with CMS concurring.

#### llm_insight
The report highlights data quality risks in Medicaid Managed Care MLR reporting and shows how gaps in internal communication can undermine oversight; strengthening data governance and cross-functional collaboration is critical to reliable capitation-rate setting.

null

The finding highlights governance and data-matching controls weaknesses in identifying incarcerated individuals within Medicaid managed care to prevent future unallowable payments.

## Latest Research Reports

### 1. Data Quality and Reporting Research Report
- slug: data-quality-and-reporting
- category: Data Quality and Reporting
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/research/data-quality-and-reporting
- published_date: 2026-07-16
- updated_date: 2026-07-16

#### description
Long-form analysis of Medicaid data quality and reporting failures, including unreported overpayments, federal-share calculation errors, and broken reconciliations between source systems and oversight reporting, with direct links to the cited audit reports.

#### executive_summary
The most consequential data-quality failures occurred where Medicaid agencies transitioned information from operational systems or partner organizations into formal financial reporting without a complete reconciliation. Across 18 reports and 26 supplied findings, auditors repeatedly identified missing records, invalid data transfers, unverified payment submissions, and late or incomplete reporting of identified overpayments.

The evidence includes large, separately reported improper amounts: a multi-state federal review found a net $61.8 million underreporting of the federal share of certain Medicaid collections, while North Carolina should have reported and returned $41.4 million in Medicaid overpayments for 12 Medicaid Fraud Control Unit (MFCU) cases in fiscal years 2020–2021. In North Carolina, some cases were omitted from reporting, while others were reported outside required timeframes. These figures should not be combined with each other or with other amounts because they concern different populations and reporting periods. [Report 44] [Report 55]

The recurring pattern is less about a single faulty report than about weak control points between source data, processing systems, and oversight reporting. The highest-priority audit targets are reconciliations of MFCU cases to Form CMS-64 reporting, federal-share calculations, overpayment classification and timeliness, managed-care pharmacy-payment reporting, eligibility-system edits, and the interfaces that move claims and electronic visit verification data into oversight records.

# Background

### 2. Managed Care Research Report
- slug: managed-care
- category: Managed Care
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/research/managed-care
- published_date: 2026-07-16
- updated_date: 2026-07-16

#### description
Long-form analysis of recurring Medicaid managed care oversight failures, with direct links to the underlying audit reports cited throughout the report.

#### executive_summary
The clearest recurring weakness is simple: Medicaid agencies often do not translate eligibility changes into timely managed care enrollment and payment actions. Across 36 managed-care-related reports and 183 findings, delayed processing of deaths, incarceration, out-of-state residence, concurrent enrollment, and other eligibility changes repeatedly allowed capitation payments to continue after eligibility should have changed or ended.

This is the broadest recurring payment-integrity pattern, with several of the largest identified exposures. The reports also show that financial risk is not confined to enrollment: auditors found payment-adjudication errors, unreliable medical loss ratio (MLR) and rate-setting data, weak corrective-action governance, and incomplete oversight of access and beneficiary protections.

The evidence includes confirmed improper or unallowable payments in several audits—for example, approximately $14 million in Maryland incarceration-related capitation payments, $11.8 million and $8.3 million in New York premium overpayments in successive review periods, and $263,186 for incarcerated Illinois enrollees. Separately, Maryland identified **$10.4 million in potentially improper** newborn supplemental payments requiring investigation and, where warranted, recovery; it should not be treated as a confirmed improper-payment amount. High-dollar residency and concurrent-enrollment figures likewise frequently describe potentially improper, estimated, or overlapping payment populations.

For audit leaders, the priority is an end-to-end control test: whether external eligibility information reaches the eligibility system, whether exceptions are resolved promptly, whether capitation stops when required, and whether improper payments are recovered. That test should be complemented by reconciliation of plan financial reporting, rate-setting inputs, service-access oversight, and corrective-action closure.

# Background

### 3. Pharmacy Benefit Managers Research Report
- slug: pharmacy-benefit-managers
- category: Pharmacy Benefit Managers
- canonical_url: https://www.medicaidintelligence.com/research/pharmacy-benefit-managers
- published_date: 2026-07-16
- updated_date: 2026-07-16

#### description
Long-form analysis of Medicaid pharmacy benefit manager oversight, pricing opacity, encounter reporting, and claims integrity risks, with direct links to the cited audit reports.

#### executive_summary
The recurring PBM oversight problem is not simply drug-price variation; it is the inability of Medicaid agencies to see, validate, and enforce what happens between claim adjudication, pharmacy payment, encounter reporting, rebate invoicing, and managed-care rate setting. Across 10 reports and 53 findings, the most consistently supported pattern is inadequate transparency and contract governance over PBM pricing, fees, adjustments, and subcontract terms.

The evidence identifies substantial control failures at several points in the pharmacy-payment lifecycle. Texas, Pennsylvania, and Oregon reported pricing or contractual structures that obscured final pharmacy payments, fees, or Medicaid-specific accountability. Other audits found incomplete encounter-data validation, weak claim edits and postpayment surveillance, missed manufacturer rebates, and insufficient assurance over the systems and third parties that process sensitive pharmacy and financial data. The highest-priority audit work is therefore transaction-level: trace PBM-adjudicated claims to pharmacy remittances and final system disposition, then reconcile the same claims through rebate invoicing and collection.

Quantified findings should be read carefully. New York reported $183.7 million in uncollected Medicaid drug rebates during its audit period, but that audit-period total may overlap with several component missed-rebate amounts and should not be added to them. Separately, Missouri and Maryland identified $572,170 in improper payments in the findings grouped as pharmacy-claim payment integrity. Most findings had no extracted dollar amount, so the financial record understates the breadth of operational risk. [Report 115] [Report 80] [Report 83]

# Background
